To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the presence within HIV- 1 quasispecies in untreated patients of ancestral sequences, dating up to 10 y before the present ones, has implications in viral evolution and pathogenesis.

the quasispecies of untreated HIV-1 infected patients contain ancestral sequences dated up to 12 years before present ones, which have important consequences in the pathogenesis of the disease and for the treatment.

(1) HIV-1 quasicpecies can contain divergent nucleotide sequence variants that have been present in the infected host since the seroconversion and (2) this phenomenon can be explained by the existence of different viral populations with different evolutionary rates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the co-existence of recent sequences, generated by the virus in the infected host, and ancestral ones, derived from the virus transmitted to the host.
the co-existence of recent sequences with ancestral nucleotide sequences within the HIV-1 quaspecies of untreated patients.
the co-existence of ancestral and recent nucleotide sequences within the HIV-1 quaspecies from untreated patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in HIV-1 infection, the coexistence of recent and ancestral sequences within a quasipatient is a frequent and important phenomenon.
, within HIV-1 provirus quasispecies from untreated patients, ancestral sequences coexist with recently evolved ones.

, in the case of HIV-1, the co-existence of ancestral and recent sequences in the viral quasispecies is a frequent phenomenon, which is not necessarily associated to double infection or samples from different tissue compartments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the co-existence within a viral population of nucleotide sequences that have evolved in parallel for several years is possible, even when there is no evidence of double infection or of different tissue compartments.

the HIV-1 quaispecies of some patients may contain a mixture of ancestral sequences and recent ones, and the presence of ancestral sequences in the quasispecies may be a common feature in the natural history of HIV-1.

in the HIV-1 infection, the presence in quasispecies of divergent nucleotides has been associated with the existence of double infections or samples taken at different times or in different tissue compartments, whereas the presence of diverged nucleotide sequences within an HIV-1 quaspecies without evidence of double infections, as the one described in our work, is a consequence of the co-existence of ancestral and recent nucleotides within the quasispecies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the quasispecies is not a homogeneous population, but a complex mixture of viral populations, including recent and ancestral sequences.
the presence of diverged nucleotide sequences in HIV-1 quaispecies does not necessarily indicate double infection, superinfection or samples from different tissue compartments.

the presence within the viral quasispecies in a single patient of divergent sequences with an early date of origin and a long time of co-existence is an indication of the presence within that quasispecies of sequences that are not derived from recent infection.
